title: AI-Driven Electrocatalyst Discovery: Integrating Machine Learning, Density Functional Theory, and High-Throughput Screening for Sustainable Energy Conversion
journal: International Journal of Soft Computing and Engineering
abstract: Efficient electrochemical processes are essential for a sustainable, low-carbon energy economy, involving hydrogen production, oxygen evolution/reduction, and carbon dioxide valorisation, all of which require high-performing electrocatalysts. Traditional catalyst development methods, which involve sequential trial-and-error synthesis and density functional theory (DFT) calculations, cannot keep pace with the combinatorial complexity of multi-metallic, single-atom, and high-entropy alloy catalysts. This review summarizes recent advances in AI-driven electrocatalyst discovery in the past five years (2020–2025) with a focus on the three pillars that have enabled this development: (1) machine learning (ML) algorithms and interpretable/explainable frameworks that extract descriptors of catalytic data that are physically meaningful; (2) the ability to couple ML with DFT using surrogate models, graph neural network interatomic potentials, and large benchmark datasets that reduce computational costs by orders of magnitude at close to DFT accuracy; and (3) high throughput screening pipelines for virtual and experimental screening, involving active learning and Bayesian optimisation, that have been applied to a diverse range of electrocatalytic reactions, including the hydrogen evolution reaction, the oxygen evolution/reduction reaction, and the carbon dioxide reduction reaction. Single-atom catalysts, perovskite oxides, and high-entropy alloys are discussed as representative examples that have helped discover new, high-performance candidates and reduced the need for one to two orders of magnitude of DFT calculations. The review also covers emerging autonomous, closed-loop ‘selfdriving’ laboratories, where robotised synthesis and characterisation are coupled with ML-driven decision-making. The review critically discusses persistent challenges in data scarcity, model interpretability and transferability across chemical spaces, and experiment-theory reproducibility, and envisions future directions such as foundation models for atomistic simulation and multimodal data fusion toward fully autonomous electrocatalyst discovery for sustainable energy conversion.

title: A Review of Artificial Intelligence Methods for Laser-Based Diagnostics: From Measurement Physics to Autonomous Sensing Systems
abstract: Laser-based diagnostic techniques are indispensable for non-intrusive, high-resolution measurements in fluid mechanics, combustion, and multiphase flows. However, modern experiments increasingly generate high-dimensional spatiotemporal datasets that strain traditional workflows and remain limited by core measurement-physics constraints, including signal-to-noise degradation, spatiotemporal resolution trade-offs, calibration uncertainty, and real-time processing demands. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) offer new capabilities for automated feature extraction, physics-aware reconstruction, Uncertainty Quantification (UQ), and real-time inference. This review synthesizes AI-enabled advances across laser velocimetry, fluorescence thermometry and species imaging, soot diagnostics, and tomographic/volumetric reconstruction. The review covers supervised and self-supervised deep learning, Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), Bayesian uncertainty-aware approaches, and generative models, emphasizing how these methods address measurement-physics limitations and what is required for reliable experimental deployment. A comparative synthesis highlights cross-modality trade-offs in accuracy, interpretability, scalability, and real-time capability, and identifies persistent challenges including generalization to unseen conditions, physical consistency, calibrated uncertainty, and closed-loop integration. The review concludes with a forward-looking framework and roadmap toward physics-aware, uncertainty-informed autonomous laser diagnostics capable of adaptive measurement strategies and real-time decision-making in complex experimental environments.

title: Toward automated discovery with generative models multimodal learning and closed loop workflows in inverse materials design
abstract: Summary: Inverse materials design is shifting materials discovery from forward prediction to targeted proposal of candidates that satisfy objectives under physical constraints. Here, we review advances in generative crystal structure modeling, multimodal learning, and closed-loop design pipelines for crystalline solids. We compare generative model classes, including variational autoencoders, normalizing flows, and autoregressive and diffusion models, focusing on their inverse design trade-offs, how physical and chemical constraints are imposed, and how reliably generated candidates survive downstream validation. We examine multimodal learning as a design interface connecting structures with properties, characterization, processing context, and scientific text and coupling these representations with latent optimization, Bayesian optimization, reinforcement learning, and active learning to guide search under limited validation budgets. We set out recurring failure modes, including surrogate exploitation, diversity collapse, distribution shift, and the stability-synthesizability gap and define a nine-rung discovery-credibility ladder, proposing a minimum reporting standard specifying evidence required to support credible materials discovery claims.

title: Mechanism–AI fusion in refining simulation software: A module-level review
abstract: Refining simulation software has remained functionally static for decades: property calculation, reaction kinetics, unit-operation modeling, and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solving modules are hard-coded, unidirectional, and cannot be calibrated online against drifting plant conditions. Purely mechanistic approaches provide irreplaceable rigor but are constrained by computational cost; purely data-driven approaches offer speed and adaptivity but lack the interpretability, generalization, and physical guarantees required for safety-critical deployment. This review examines how mechanism–AI fusion—encompassing physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), reduced-order models (ROMs), operator learning, and closure-model augmentation—is reshaping these functional modules at the architectural level. We propose a module-level taxonomy that maps each fusion strategy to the specific simulation module it transforms, and we distinguish this paradigm from related concepts (hybrid modeling, physics-informed machine learning, grey-box modeling, and digital twins) by specifying the bidirectional information flows between mechanistic and AI components. A systematic literature survey following PRISMA-style methodology identified 133 references from Web of Science, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore (2000–2025). We provide enhanced comparative tables that include training cost, data requirements, extrapolation ability, uncertainty quantification (UQ), scalability, and industrial maturity for each method class. Industrial software benchmarking is presented as a qualitative comparison rather than a subjective ranking. Three industrial case studies (gasifier, FCC unit, distillation column) are analyzed with explicit baselines, deployment durations, and performance indicators, clearly identifying vendor-reported versus independently verified data. We discuss emerging topics—AI-native scientific software, foundation models for scientific computing, autonomous engineering agents, trustworthy and explainable AI, verification & validation (V&V), and MLOps for scientific applications—that will shape the next decade. The review concludes with graded findings (verified, supported, emerging, conceptual, and policy-level) to clearly distinguish established results from industrial observations and conceptual proposals. The central finding is that mechanism–AI fusion transforms refining simulation software from a fixed-algorithm tool into an adaptive multi-fidelity platform, but the transition from advisory and optimization applications to safety-critical closed-loop control requires standardized V&V protocols, UQ frameworks, and process-industry-specific safety governance that do not yet exist.

title: AIMNet2-rxn: A machine-learned potential for generalized reaction modeling on a millions-of-pathways scale
abstract: Mechanistic modeling of chemical transformations offers a compelling basis for understanding reactivity and allows for prediction of reaction outcomes before attempting experiments. Despite progress in machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs), we demonstrate that available models lack the accuracy for diverse reaction modeling. With this motivation, we developed a general MLIP for mechanistic modeling of closed-shell carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen reactions, AIMNet2-rxn, using a dataset of ∼4.7 × 10 6 range-separated density functional theory calculations. AIMNet2-rxn enables reaction modeling ∼10 6 faster than the reference quantum mechanical (QM) methods while substantially outperforming graph-based ML, reaffirming the value using three-dimensional chemical information for training. On a test suite of well-known reaction mechanisms—such as amide formation, proton transfers, and pericyclics—AIMNet2-rxn yields 1 to 2 kilocalories per mole accuracy across reaction coordinates without retraining or system-specific fine-tuning. To exploit graphics processing unit parallelism and AIMNet2-rxn efficiency, we introduce a batched nudged elastic band procedure that readily achieves minimum energy pathway search on a millions-of-reactions scale. To demonstrate complex reaction characterization, the thermodynamics of an 11-step pathway producing hydroxymethylfurfural, the experimentally observed major product of glucose pyrolysis, is evaluated. Overall, the accuracy and efficiency afforded by AIMNet2-rxn create opportunities in high-throughput reaction discovery and deep reaction network analysis that would be infeasible with QM methods.

title: Tuning Pore Confinement and Chemistry of Fluorine-Free Membranes
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Abstract The design of low-temperature fuel cells and electrolyzers involving proton exchange membranes (PEMs) has been dominated by the exceptional performance and industrial dominance of Nafion. With emerging regulations banning the use of fluorinated compounds, the search for F-free alternatives must be accelerated. Here, we optimize a fluorine-free, sustainable, and low-cost liquid crystalline poly(epichlorohydrin)membrane, based on the identification of key descriptors for proton mobility obtained using machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) derived from first-principles calculations for extensive molecular dynamics. Proton transfer is controlled by the interplay between water confinement and internal pore chemistry. This allows us to modify the active functional groups so that they directly participate in the proton diffusion process, increasing three times the diffusion rate in the membrane, thus being closer to Nafion standards. This work provides key descriptors for a targeted design approach essential for catalyzing the commercial development of next-generation fluorine-free PEMs.

title: Modeling Phase Separation in Polymer-Derived Silicon Carbonitride Ceramics through Extended Machine Learning Molecular Dynamics
abstract: Abstract Polymer-derived ceramics combine the thermal stability of ceramics with the versatile properties of carbon domains, but modeling their atomic-scale evolution during processing remains elusive because of the limitations of traditional computational methods. To address this issue, here, we develop and apply a machine learning interatomic potential for hydrogen-containing silicon carbonitride-based (SiCNH) ceramics, trained on a diversified database of over 9000 configurations─including amorphous models, high-temperature states, surfaces, and crystal structure predictions─to capture the full complexity of these materials. This potential enables large-scale molecular dynamics simulations of 8000-atom systems, revealing the atomic-scale evolution of the polymer-derived ceramic during thermal treatment. A key result of this work is the occurrence of a phase separation, where carbon domains progressively nucleate from the amorphous SiCN matrix during thermal processing, forming distinct graphene-like sheets while preserving the integrity of the ceramic network. The resulting models reproduce the experimental atomic pair distribution functions, supporting our approach and providing microscopic explanations for the material combination of the ceramic and graphitic properties. In this process, defective 5- and/or 7-member carbon rings mediate the transformation to stable 6-member aromatic structures. These findings provide atomic-scale information about the thermal stability and structural transformation pathways of polymer-derived ceramics and demonstrate the applicability of the methodology to complex amorphous systems at experimentally relevant scales.

title: Closing the learning loop in lithium–sulfur batteries through physics-informed and trustworthy artificial intelligence
abstract: Lithium–sulfur (Li–S) batteries combine a high theoretical specific energy with low-cost active materials, yet their development remains constrained by coupled reaction pathways, mobile intermediates, lithium-metal instability, and a large design space that changes with loading, electrolyte inventory, temperature, format, and cycling history. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a way to connect these variables, but most published demonstrations remain isolated within small computational datasets, literature-derived tables, or single-laboratory cell series. This review develops an evidence-first, closed-loop framework for AI-enabled Li–S research that links observation, learning, decision, validation, and model updating. It critically examines data infrastructure, text and multimodal extraction, descriptor learning, catalyst and electrolyte design, physics-informed state inference, degradation prognosis, autonomous experimentation, and digital twins. The available evidence shows that machine learning (ML) can compress high-dimensional calculations, recover useful structure–property relations, and predict selected cell outcomes within bounded domains. However, ML has not yet demonstrated robust transfer across laboratories, cell formats, or practical operating conditions. The main barriers are incomplete metadata, non-independent data splits, uncertain labels, weak uncertainty calibration, and limited prospective validation. To address these gaps, the review introduces a minimum data schema, an evidence-fidelity pathway that separates proxy prediction from decision-grade evidence, task-specific benchmarking requirements, and a minimum viable digital-twin architecture for Li–S cells. The central conclusion is that AI becomes decision-grade only when its predictions are physically credible, uncertainty-aware, experimentally actionable, and iteratively validated.

title: Advanced engineering of inorganic semiconductor nanowires: Materials-by-design for next-generation green energy technologies
abstract: Inorganic semiconductor nanowires (NWs) provide an unusually versatile platform for green-energy technologies because composition, crystal phase, defects, interfaces, morphology, and dimensionality can be engineered across multiple length scales. This review critically examines how these coupled design variables govern charge generation and transport, surface recombination, catalytic activity, ion diffusion, thermal transport, and operational stability. Rather than cataloguing individual materials, we identify transferable structure–property–performance relationships across photovoltaics, photoelectrochemical water splitting, photocatalysis, electrochemical energy storage, and thermoelectric conversion. A central conclusion is that nanoscale advantages are intrinsically conditional: reduced dimensions can enhance light trapping, carrier collection, reaction kinetics, and strain accommodation, but simultaneously intensify surface recombination, interfacial instability, defect sensitivity, and integration losses. We therefore evaluate competing engineering strategies in terms of these trade-offs and their implications for device-scale performance, durability, manufacturability, and sustainability. Recent advances in operando characterization, multiscale simulation, density functional theory, machine learning, and active learning are further assessed as tools for connecting synthesis conditions with experimentally validated material states and functional performance. Particular attention is given to the remaining gap between idealized computational predictions and structurally complex experimental NWs. Finally, we identify reproducibility, standardized data, device integration, scalable manufacturing, long-term stability, and uncertainty-aware human-supervised automation as critical requirements for translating semiconductor NWs from laboratory optimization toward deployable green-energy systems.

title: Cross-chemistry battery state-of-health estimation from adaptive partial charging using interpretable physics-informed Efficient Kolmogorov-Arnold networks
abstract: ABSTRACT Accurate, robust state-of-health (SOH) estimation is essential for safe battery operation and second-life deployment, yet most existing methods depend on fixed feature extraction windows rarely available in real-world charging and offer limited interpretability or cross-chemistry generalization. To address these issues, we propose the physics-informed efficient Kolmogorov-Arnold network (PI-EKAN), which estimates SOH from adaptive partial charging. Prefix-specific Bayesian optimization (PS-BO) selects the most informative state-of-charge window for each chemistry and extracts seven voltage-based descriptors; this feed-coupled solution and dynamics networks are trained under a bounded uncertainty-weighted objective that keeps the data, physics, and monotonicity constraints balanced. Across eight datasets, PI-EKAN reaches an average MAPE of 0.466%, an RMSE of 0.529%, and an R² above 0.979, cutting MAPE by 35.6% relative to a physics-informed baseline while using only 1,800 parameters, far fewer than comparable recurrent Kolmogorov-Arnold models. PS-BO identifies chemistry-specific charging windows that stay informative under restricted SOC visibility, reduced sampling frequency, and simulated battery-management-system errors. In cross-chemistry tests, adapting the pretrained model with one labeled target cell cuts average MAPE from 6.35% source-only transfer to 1.19% using hybrid low-rank EKAN-LoRA fine-tuning with half the trainable parameters across sixteen transfer pairs. Component ablation identifies the bounded adaptive weighting as the key stabilizing element, and post-hoc attribution and learned-spline analyses consistently rank voltage-shape descriptors as the leading inputs, indicating that the model captures degradation-related structure rather than dataset artifacts. These results establish PI-EKAN as a compact, interpretable, chemistry-transferable framework for SOH estimation from the incomplete charging data real battery systems produce.

title: General-purpose LLMs as constrained crystal composition generators
abstract: Abstract The targeted discovery of inorganic materials remains challenging due to the vastness of compositional design spaces and the high cost of exhaustive screening. Task-specific generative artificial intelligence represents a particularly efficient alternative to screening, yet demands tedious collection of training data before providing real benefit. General-purpose large language models (LLMs) have recently shown tremendous potential for the targeted generation of single, optimal materials compositions without the need for task-specific fine-tuning. However, it is unclear whether LLMs generally pose an advantage compared to specialized generative models, in particular in large design spaces. Here, we demonstrate that such models are capable of covering entire regions of the targeted property space effectively and systematically. Using Elpasolite materials as an established benchmark for generative tasks in large chemical spaces, we find that an iterative prompt-and-response framework is able to recover on average 96% of all low-energy Elpasolites in the target region. This performance, driven mainly by iterative in-context learning, surpasses the generative abilities of previous, task-specific models. Our results establish general-purpose LLMs as flexible and accessible components for inverse materials design workflows.

title: Digital twins for energy wells through multiscale physics-data fusion: Review, challenges, and a conceptual framework
abstract: Energy wells underpin critical technologies in the global energy transition, including geothermal energy extraction, carbon capture and storage, and underground hydrogen storage. In recent years, digital twin (DT) concepts have been increasingly explored to support well design, monitoring, and integrity management. However, most existing DT implementations for energy wells remain limited in scope and maturity, with incomplete integration of multiscale physics, evolving field data, and adaptive operational decision support. These limitations arise from heavy reliance on high-fidelity physics-based simulations with prohibitive computational costs, or on purely data-driven models that exhibit limited generalizability under evolving geological and operational conditions. To clarify the current state of the field, this paper first reviews recent DT developments for energy wells across oil and gas, geothermal, and subsurface energy storage applications. Building on this, we further synthesize advances in molecular dynamics, pore-scale simulation, continuum-scale thermo–hydro–mechanical–chemical modeling, and physics-informed machine learning, highlighting how multiscale physical processes governing clay–cement–fluid interactions, deformation, damage, and transport are currently treated in isolation. Motivated by these gaps, we propose a conceptual multiscale physics–data fusion DT framework for energy wells. The framework outlines an integrated architecture in which molecular- and mesoscale descriptors are systematically upscaled into continuum constitutive relationships, while top-down geological and operational constraints are incorporated to ensure cross-scale physical consistency. A central artificial intelligence layer is introduced to conceptually combine physics-informed surrogate models with ensemble-based data assimilation of heterogeneous monitoring data (e.g., pressure, temperature, deformation, and acoustic responses), enabling real-time updating primarily at the continuum-scale THMC and surrogate-model layers, while molecular- and pore-scale modules provide offline mechanistic priors and event-triggered feedback within a hierarchical multiscale DT architecture. An illustrative lifecycle workflow based on a geological CO 2 storage well is presented to demonstrate how the proposed framework could, in principle, support design optimization, operational anomaly diagnosis, and long-term integrity assessment. This study provides a unifying methodological foundation for the future development of predictive and data-adaptive DTs for subsurface energy systems.

title: A review on foundation models for polymer informatics
abstract: Foundation models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for learning transferable knowledge from broad, heterogeneous data and adapting them to diverse downstream tasks, driving a growing interest in AI-accelerated scientific discovery. In polymer science, this paradigm offers a promising route beyond conventional machine learning methods that are often confined to isolated tasks and struggle to generalize under data scarcity and across heterogeneous downstream settings. Polymer foundation models (PFMs), however, are not merely general scientific foundation models applied to polymer datasets. They must address representation, generation, transfer, and evaluation challenges specific to polymer informatics. This review synthesizes recent progress in PFMs for representation learning and generative modeling, spanning models designed for polymer systems and those adapted from general foundation models. We organize this review around two stages: (1) polymer modeling as the foundation, covering representations, datasets, model architectures, and pretraining objectives; and (2) downstream applications, evaluation, and adaptation. By synthesizing recent progress, open challenges, and future directions, this review outlines a roadmap toward robust and generalizable foundation models for polymer informatics.

title: Beyond Scalar Objectives: Expert-Feedback-Driven Autonomous Experimentation for Scientific Discovery at the Nanoscale
abstract: Abstract Self-driving laboratories or autonomous experimentation are emerging as transformative platforms for accelerating scientific discovery. Bayesian optimization (BO) is among the most widely used machine learning frameworks in self-driving laboratories, but these BO-based frameworks rely on predefined scalar descriptors to guide experimentation. This limits their ability to handle complex phenomena that are difficult to formalize as scalar descriptors. In many situations, the determination of an appropriate scalar descriptor can be challenging, and may fail to capture subtle yet scientifically important phenomena apparent to experts with interdisciplinary insight. This problem is particularly pronounced in nanoscale imaging experiments, where strong local heterogeneity, multidimensional observations, and emergent physical behaviors often cannot be effectively represented using scalar metrics. To overcome this limitation, here we develop deep-kernel pairwise learning (DKPL), an approach for autonomous microscopy experiments which incorporates human expertise and interdisciplinary scientific knowledge into an active learning loop. Instead of relying on explicit scalar objectives, DKPL enables experts to directly evaluate which experimental output is more promising using interdisciplinary knowledge. DKPL then learns a latent utility function from these expert judgments to guide subsequent autonomous microscopy experiments. We demonstrate DKPL’s performance in learning physically meaningful nanoscale structures in lead titanate thin films while effectively prioritizing high-information measurement regions using an experimental model dataset with known ground truth. We further apply DKPL to analyze the character of ferroelectric domain walls, where we find DKPL capable of distinguishing between high and low characteristic domain-wall angles in lead zirconium titanate, and able to discover both head-to-head and tail-to-tail domain-wall character in erbium manganite. Autonomous experiments in mixed-phase bismuth ferrite also demonstrate DKPL’s ability to link material structure with their properties in on-the-fly measurements. This development demonstrates an approach to integrate expert knowledge into autonomous microscopy experiments across a variety of material systems, and demonstrates a pathway toward expert-guided self-driving laboratories capable of addressing scientific problems beyond the limits of scalar-metrics-driven learning.

title: SSCHA-based evolutionary crystal structure prediction at finite temperatures with account for quantum nuclear motion
abstract: Abstract Reliable crystal structure prediction (CSP) at finite temperatures, including quantum anharmonic effects, remains challenging but is particularly important for systems containing light atoms such as superconducting hydrides. Here, we integrate machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) with the stochastic self-consistent harmonic approximation (SSCHA) to enable evolutionary CSP on the quantum anharmonic free-energy landscape. Using LaH 10 as a test case, we compare three approaches: (i) active-learning MLIPs (AL-MLIPs) trained on the fly, (ii) universal MLIPs (uMLIPs), and (iii) temperature-dependent effective potentials (TDEPs) trained on SSCHA ensemble data. AL-MLIPs correctly predict the cubic Fm $$\bar{3}$$ 3 ¯ m phase but require thermodynamic perturbation theory corrections for consistent results. The foundation uMLIP Mattersim-5m enables SSCHA-based CSP without per-structure training, but fine-tuning is required for higher accuracy. Temperature-dependent effective potentials trained on SSCHA data enable accurate and very efficient CSP for large unit cells on the quantum anharmonic free-energy landscape. We demonstrate that quantum anharmonicity simplifies the free-energy landscape and is essential for the correct energy ranking of LaH 10 structures.

title: Integration of density functional theory and machine learning for materials discovery in energy applications
abstract: The global transition toward clean and renewable energy systems demands the rapid identification of novel functional materials for hydrogen production, photocatalysis, CO₂ reduction, and electrochemical energy storage. Traditional experimental trial and error approaches, combined with computationally expensive standalone density functional theory (DFT) calculations, have long constrained the pace of materials discovery. The convergence of machine learning (ML) and DFT has emerged as a transformative paradigm that accelerates the identification, screening, and validation of energy-relevant materials. This review critically surveys the integration of DFT and ML across the energy-materials landscape. Examine how DFT generated datasets, encompassing bandgap values, formation energies, adsorption energies, and electronic structure descriptors, serve as the foundation for training predictive ML models, and delineate the methodological pipeline that connects them. The roles of curated materials databases, including the Materials Project, the Open Quantum Materials Database (OQMD), and AFLOW, in enabling data-driven discovery are discussed alongside the workflow-automation frameworks that operationalise them. Applications spanning the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), photocatalytic water splitting, CO₂ reduction, and lithium-ion battery materials are reviewed. Current challenges, including data quality and coverage, DFT accuracy limitations, model interpretability, out of distribution generalisation, and the reproducibility of several landmark large-scale demonstrations, are addressed, and future directions toward autonomous materials discovery platforms integrating artificial intelligence, robotics, and quantum computing are outlined together with their present-day limitations and motivating open problems. The DFT - ML framework has matured from a proof of concept into an important engine of energy materials discovery. DFT - ML integration enables accelerated discovery and screening of functional energy materials. Graph-based learning provides efficient prediction of key DFT-derived materials properties. Active learning couples ML screening with targeted DFT calculations for efficient materials exploration. High-throughput workflows and open databases establish scalable, data-driven materials discovery pipelines. Critical assessment identifies data, accuracy, interpretability, reproducibility, and generalisation challenges.

title: Distilling First-Principles Accuracy into Compact Machine Learning Potentials for Condensed-Phase Chemistry
journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation
abstract: Abstract Accurate machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have made first-principles-quality potential energy surfaces increasingly accessible for condensed-phase chemistry, but their inference cost can still limit the sampling needed to compute experimentally relevant observables. In this work, we use knowledge distillation to construct compact “student” models that retain the accuracy of much larger “teacher” models obtained through either finetuning of foundation models or Δ-learning. The resulting students reduce production simulation cost by approximately an order of magnitude, making high-accuracy sampling practical for challenging condensed-phase problems. We demonstrate this across three problems of increasing sampling complexity: finite-temperature NPT simulations of ice Ih, classical and path-integral simulations of liquid water over 240–370 K, and path-integral umbrella-sampling simulations of water dissociation at the anatase TiO2(101)/water interface. When compared, the distilled students reproduce the target observables of their teachers more reliably than equally compact models trained only on the available reference data. The liquid water student, distilled from a Δ-learned CCSD(T)-quality teacher, reproduces thermodynamic, structural, transport, and nuclear quantum effects over the full temperature range studied. At the TiO2/water interface, knowledge distillation makes PIMD umbrella sampling practical and shows that nuclear quantum effects lower the dissociation barrier by approximately 2 kcal/mol and shift the molecular–dissociated free energy difference into closer agreement with recent solid-state 17O NMR measurements. Our work demonstrates how knowledge distillation can make accurate MLIPs practical for the sampling methods needed to connect condensed-phase reaction thermodynamics with experiment, notably for interfacial chemistry and catalysis.

title: From Trial-and-Error to Closed-Loop Design: A Data-Driven Review on Biomass-Derived Carbon for Supercapacitors
abstract: Supercapacitors are vital for sustainable energy storage, and biomass-derived carbons are promising electrode materials owing to their low cost, renewability, and inherent hierarchical porosity. However, their electrochemical performance arises from a complex interplay of pore architecture, graphitization degree, and heteroatom doping, making trial-and-error optimization inefficient. This review adopts a data-driven perspective, systematically covering the entire value chain (from precursor selection and carbonization to pore engineering, surface modification, and characterization) while emphasizing how each variable can be quantified as input features for machine learning (ML). We discuss the mechanistic roles of structure, graphitization, and surface chemistry in regulating ion transport, electron conduction, and charge storage, and summarize common characterization (Raman, XRD, XPS, FTIR, BET) and electrochemical (CV, GCD, EIS) techniques. Critically, we highlight several problematic practices: the misleading “green” activation narrative, scalability limits of templating, non-linear trade-offs in chasing ultra-high surface area and heavy doping, oversimplified interpretation of the Raman I D / I G ratio, and deceptive reliance on three-electrode data for device-level predictions. To overcome these, we advocate for a closed-loop, data-driven design framework that integrates standardized databases, active learning, and inverse design to guide the rational development of biomass-derived carbon electrodes. This framework integrates ML not as an add-on but as the central engine connecting precursor–process–structure–performance relationships. Realizing the full potential of biomass-derived carbons demands a cultural shift from pursuing idealized metrics toward reproducibility, scalability, and rigorous device-relevant validation. By merging closed-loop data-driven discovery with mechanistic understanding, the field can effectively bridge the gap between laboratory findings and practical supercapacitor technologies.

title: Large language models, ChatGPT, and beyond: A new paradigm for condition monitoring and prognosis in power and energy systems
abstract: Large language models and related foundation models offer new capabilities for interpreting heterogeneous information, retrieving engineering knowledge, and supporting high-level decision processes in power and energy systems. This Perspective examines their role in condition monitoring and prognostics and health management, with particular emphasis on remaining useful life estimation. To support language and multimodal model interpretation of structured and validated estimates, we propose a digital twin-centric architecture comprising physics-guided hybrid estimation, digital twin synchronization, rule-governed semantic translation, foundation model reasoning, output validation, and human supervision. The specific contribution is threefold. First, the proposed layering principle distinguishes physically consistent estimation, system integration, and higher-level reasoning functions. Second, an auditable semantic interface is defined to encode health indicators, degradation states, remaining useful life distributions, uncertainty information, operating context, provenance, retrieved evidence, and permitted reasoning scope. Third, a deployment-oriented reliability framework relates physical consistency, digital twin consistency, explanation fidelity, uncertainty preservation, robustness, traceability, safe deferral, latency, data sensitivity, and computational requirements to edge, on premises, cloud, and hybrid implementations. An illustrative battery state-of-health and remaining useful life use case demonstrates the resulting information flow. The foundation model layer is primarily intended for slow-timescale, human-supervised functions such as diagnostic explanation, degradation interpretation, maintenance prioritization, inspection planning, and fleet-level assessment, rather than protection or real-time control. The Perspective also examines complementary roles for small language models, tiny recursive models, world models, large language models, and multimodal foundation models and identifies priorities for their reliable evaluation and deployment in power and energy prognostics and health management.

title: A Comprehensive Review of Battery State of Health Estimation: Methods, Challenges and Future Perspectives
journal: International Journal of Automotive Science And Technology
abstract: Lithium-ion battery state of health (SOH) cannot be measured directly and must be inferred from capacity, resistance, voltage, current, temperature, and usage history. This structured narrative review integrates degradation mechanisms with feature-based, model-based, data-driven, and physics-informed/hybrid estimation methods, and evaluates them against validation design, chemistry dependence, uncertainty, computational burden, and on-board feasibility. The literature was updated through targeted searches of Crossref-indexed publisher platforms, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink/Nature, Wiley Online Library, and MDPI; 117 unique publications, institutional reports, and regulatory documents were retained after duplicate removal and relevance screening. Reported errors are treated as study-specific results rather than universal characteristics of method families. The synthesis shows that no single estimator is uniformly superior: feature-based diagnostics provide physical insight but require informative and low-noise operating segments; equivalent-circuit observers are compatible with embedded implementation but depend on model adaptation; data-driven models can achieve low error within their validation domain but require rigorous cross-cell and cross-condition testing; and physics-informed or hybrid approaches offer a promising compromise when their added complexity is justified. Future progress depends on transparent validation, uncertain-aware estimation, chemistry transfer, compact edge implementation, multimodal sensing, and auditable life-cycle data under emerging battery regulations.

title: Reinforcement Learning on the Discrete Composition Channel of a Crystal Generator: Validated Gains and Reward Hacking
abstract: Inverse materials design is a long-standing goal of computational materials discovery. Generative models for crystalline materials are typically trained to match the distribution of a structure database, while nothing in their training objective points them at specific design goals such as targeted properties. We use group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) to align a generative model based on stochastic interpolants and discrete flow matching with general black-box reward functions through reinforcement learning. Atom types are generated by a discrete flow and the policy gradient of our generalization of GRPO directly acts on the likelihoods of the atom-type transitions, which differentiates our work from previous reinforcement-learning approaches for diffusion and flow-based generative models of crystalline materials. We introduce a reward function that raises the yield of metastable, unique and novel structures (mSUN) from 13.4% for the pretrained model to 45.5% for the reinforced model, as evaluated by a community benchmark. Our reward also improves the performance of a reinforcement learning framework for crystalline materials based on latent denoising diffusion models. At the same time, we find that directly reinforcing atom-type transition likelihoods enables reward exploitation that has to be prevented with explicit guards. The same analysis also exposes a gap in the community metric. Single-element structures in distinct packings are counted as metastable, unique and novel materials and inflate mSUN without yielding any new compounds. A stability claim is only as good as its reference hull. We report every result split by the number of reference phases behind it and argue that benchmarks should do the same.

title: GEODE: Symmetry-Preserving Cartesian Diffusion for Crystal Generation
abstract: Most known inorganic crystals exhibit symmetric atomic arrangements, yet generative models often fail to reproduce them. Explicitly enforcing these symmetries has so far yielded fewer stable and novel structures than unconstrained generation. We introduce Generative Equivariant Orbit Diffusion Engine (GEODE), to our knowledge the first model to combine coordinate and lattice diffusion in Cartesian space. GEODE first samples symmetry templates, then jointly generates the lattice, atomic coordinates and atom types while preserving the specified symmetry with a novel Wyckoff-constrained loss. Cartesian diffusion gives coordinate noise a consistent physical scale that we empirically demonstrate improves performance. Unconditional generation achieves a metastable, unique and novel (mSUN) rate of 11.9%, compared with 7.7% for the next best symmetry-aware model. We also introduce sampling time template filtering, which increases mSUN by ~6% without retraining, making GEODE competitive with leading symmetry-agnostic models. Template selection also enables joint symmetry and property guidance, which we demonstrate through classifier-free guidance of permittivity.

title: Artificial intelligence in microplastic and nanoplastic research: State-of-Art review from automated detection to environmental fate modeling
abstract: Microplastic and nanoplastic research has entered a data-intensive phase in which analytical throughput, interlaboratory comparability, and environmental interpretability determine whether monitoring results can support mechanistic understanding and management decisions. This critical review evaluates where artificial intelligence (AI) adds analytical value and where performance claims remain fragile across sampling, imaging, spectroscopy, multimodal characterization, environmental fate and transport, engineered treatment, toxicity, and risk assessment. Rather than treating reported accuracy as a sufficient indicator of readiness, competing AI approaches are compared according to label provenance, robustness to domain shift, external validation, uncertainty quantification, computational burden, and feasibility for routine laboratories. Computer vision and spectral classifiers can reduce manual screening under controlled acquisition, but performance commonly deteriorates across instruments, staining protocols, particle aging states, size ranges, and environmental matrices; visual classification alone cannot establish polymer identity. Explainable AI is useful only when attribution is stable and chemically interpretable, while physics-informed learning is most defensible when mass conservation, boundary conditions, and dimensionally consistent transport equations constrain model behavior. Public image and spectral resources are expanding, but they remain fragmented, single-modality, and incompletely standardized. Regulatory translation is further limited by insufficient proficiency testing, locked model validation, traceable version control, and demonstrated equivalence to accepted analytical methods. A tiered implementation framework is therefore proposed in which AI supports prescreening, uncertainty-based triage, spectroscopic confirmation, mechanistic modeling, and auditable decision support rather than operating as an unverified stand-alone classifier.

title: Polymer Informatics in the Era of Foundation Models: From Representation to Autonomous Design
abstract: Foundation models, pretrained on broad datasets and adapted to multiple tasks, offer a way to reuse chemical knowledge across polymer property prediction and inverse design. Realizing this opportunity requires connecting learned representations to materials whose properties also depend on molecular populations, formulation, processing, and measurement conditions. Here, we review advances in polymer foundation models and the data, representations, and experimental workflows that support their use in materials design. We organize these developments around the polymer material state, a description linking chemical identity to molecular distributions, architecture, morphology, and preparation history relevant to a target property. This organization connects data resources and pretraining strategies to questions about what models learn, how that knowledge transfers, and which experimental choices it can support. We compare learning objectives and adaptation methods, examine representations of polymer chemistry and state, and follow inverse design from candidate generation through synthesis and processing to validation. Pretrained models now support prediction across multiple properties and generation for specified targets, with selected polymer candidates reaching synthesis and thermal characterization. Broader polymer design campaigns show how precursor accessibility, polymerization outcomes, and specimen preparation influence whether a predicted advantage becomes a measured material response. Building on this evidence, we discuss opportunities to combine chemical pretraining with richer sample information and to assess transfer across polymer families, preparation conditions, and experimental campaigns. The resulting synthesis connects model development to a practical objective for polymer informatics: reducing the new experimentation needed to obtain materials with reproducible, targeted performance.

title: Improved electrostatic machine learning embedding ML/MM scheme for a phosphoryl transfer reaction
abstract: The promise of hybrid machine learning/molecular mechanics (ML/MM) simulations is to provide QM/MM-quality free energy profiles at a fraction of the cost. One of the challenges is to accurately treat the interaction between the ML subsystem and the MM environment. Here we test the Electrostatic ML Embedding (EMLE) scheme on a minimal model of RNA cleavage in water, which is already challenging due to a doubly charged reactant dissociating into two anions. The original scheme, a MACE potential embedded by an independent EMLE model, is compared with a new EMLE–MACE architecture, in which a single equivariant network predicts the gas-phase energy together with the atomic charges, valence widths, polarizabilities and static dipoles required by the embedding. The models were trained by active learning against M06-2X/def2- TZVP data, with structures selected by query-by-committee from the ML/MM dynamics itself. About 1500 single point calculations were sufficient for stable 100 ps umbrella sampling simulations in 73 windows along the reaction pathway. The EMLE–MACE profile reproduces the reference DFT/MM profile within its sampling error, including a metastable pentacoordinate intermediate. Energy decomposition shows that the static dipoles are essential: without them the static error stays above chemical accuracy even for an ideally trained model, due to the irreducible error of approximating electron density with spherical atoms.

title: OxiGen: Oxidation-State-Aware Crystal Generation
abstract: Generative models have the potential to accelerate inorganic materials discovery by enabling inverse design, but generating experimentally realisable crystals remains challenging. Oxidation states are widely used to assess the compositional validity of crystals and guide inorganic materials discovery. While existing generative models for crystals can generate materials with charge-neutral oxidation-state assignments, they poorly reproduce the distributions of oxidation states observed in synthesised materials. To address this limitation, we propose OxiGen, an oxidation-state-aware crystal diffusion model that explicitly represents oxidation states during generation. OxiGen enforces global charge neutrality by construction using a structured output layer with exact inference over a finite-state automaton. Empirically, OxiGen substantially improves oxidation-state fidelity, generates the highest rate of stable, unique, and novel crystals among evaluated methods, and maintains high compositional validity even under property conditioning.

title: Machine-Learning-Driven Simulations of Hyperthermal Atomic Oxygen Impacts on (0001) Al2O3 for Low-Altitude Satellite Design.
abstract: In Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO), spacecraft encounter residual atmosphere primarily composed of atomic oxygen (AO). The drag and operational lifetime of these spacecraft are determined by the interaction between AO and the surface, which for aluminum is a passivation layer of Al2O3. We present a blueprint for developing machine-learned interatomic potentials for reactive gas-surface systems. Gaussian-Moment Neural Networks, implemented in apax, are trained using an active learning workflow that incorporates a spin-state switching scheme. This approach accounts for the triplet-to-singlet transition that AO undergoes upon adsorption, a process usually neglected in machine-learned potential studies. This methodology enables the simulation of thousands of hyperthermal impacts on (0001) Al2O3 at orbital velocity with near-first-principles accuracy for systems four times larger and four orders of magnitude cheaper than ab initio molecular dynamics. Alumina is not an inert surface. Most impacting atoms adsorb rather than reflect, and with continuous exposure, the surface reaches a dynamic steady state where ∼14% of the binding sites are occupied. The surface remains intact. Atoms desorb primarily as O2 formed by recombination, indicating that surface chemistry, rather than simple scattering, governs the energy transfer during impact. Conventional spacecraft drag models assume that impacting atoms desorb thermally in equilibrium with the surface. Our findings demonstrate that this assumption is invalid for alumina. We determine an energy accommodation coefficient of 0.61, which is lower than the 0.82 to 1.0 range measured on actual spacecraft surfaces. This discrepancy quantifies the effect of technical surface roughness. When scaling the simulated momentum transfer to the European Space Agency's GOCE satellite, the measured reentry drag force is reproduced within a factor of 1.8. Since an atomically smooth surface still exhibits strong energy accommodation through chemical bond formation, effective drag reduction in VLEO requires materials that are both atomically smooth and chemically inert.

title: Tractable and Thermodynamically Consistent p K a Prediction via First-Dissociation Aggregation
abstract: Abstract Ionization governs molecular behavior, yet predicting aqueous pKa accurately and tractably remains a fundamental challenge. Rigorous ensemble methods require enumerating a protonation-state space that grows exponentially with the number of ionizable sites, while fast graph predictors return numbers without thermodynamic consistency. Here we derive an exact thermodynamic identity showing that the macroscopic first-dissociation constant is fully determined by protonated-microstate populations and unique first-deprotonation events, eliminating the deprotonated ensemble algebraically and reducing aggregation to O(n+E) operations. We implement this identity in DTi-pKa, a dual-head graph neural network whose free-energy and dissociation heads are coupled by thermodynamic constraints. On four external benchmarks (355 molecules), DTi-pKa achieves a pooled MAE of 0.5665 pKa units, with 0.6285 on the 169 records lacking training-cache matches, while providing site-resolved micro-pKa values and protonation-state populations. Controlled ablations show that constraint placement at the level of the reported macroscopic equilibrium matters more than microscopic label precision—a design principle transferable to physics-informed machine learning beyond chemistry. Closure diagnostics expose numerical self-consistency as an open frontier, which we report transparently. By replacing an intractable computation with a physical identity, DTi-pKa unifies macroscopic accuracy and microscopic interpretability in a single framework.

title: Artificial intelligence for scanning probe microscopy: From data analysis to autonomous experimentation
abstract: Abstract Advanced scanning probe microscopy (SPM) measurements have traditionally required highly specialized skills, but the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning has begun to transform how SPM is operated. This review surveys AI methods applied to SPM, organized by technique rather than chronology: unsupervised learning for feature extraction, support vector machines for real-time classification, convolutional neural networks for image analysis, Bayesian optimization for experiment planning, reinforcement learning for atomic and molecular manipulation, and object detection for feature localization. The emerging use of large language models as natural-language interfaces for microscope operation is discussed as a distinct topic. For each method, the operating principles and representative SPM applications are presented. This method-centric organization enables direct comparison of AI approaches applied to similar SPM tasks and clarifies the complementary roles---perception, decision-making, control, and orchestration---that each technique plays in integrated autonomous SPM systems.
